text.p: World oil prices held onto healthy levels on Thursday and ignored evidence of plentiful supply to consolidate the gains made in the last week.
By 1607 GMT the June futures contract for bellwether Brent crude, which expires today, was traded just five cents lower at $19.46.
It finished yesterday only 12 cents lower, still close to the peak reached on Monday after a five-day rally that pushed it up nearly two dollars to a two-month high.
In New York the West Texas Intermediate futures contract was down five cents at $21.34 in thin trade.
"This is a market which is very, very neutral at the moment," said Peter Gignoux, energy analyst at Smith Barney. "There are not many talking points."
Market professionals said crude was supported by futures buying from institutional funds, and by technical factors triggered on the charts that track the value of benchmark hydrocarbon derivatives.

"The technicals have taken over completely," said one oil products trader. "There is bearish news out there but the market is still perky. When the funds buy millions of lots they have their way, whatever the fundamentals."
Oil markets have spent the last week turning away from bad news.
They soared last Friday, despite statistics from the West's energy watchdog, the International Energy Agency, that suggested crude production would outstrip demand this summer.
Crude continued its climb on Monday and largely held its strength on Wednesday, despite U.S. inventory data that showed a dramatic rise in oil stocks, which would normally depress prices.

On Thursday news that North Sea crude supply would not be as badly affected as anticipated by maintenance programmes and that a major European refinery in Rotterdam was cutting its throughput barely dented prices.
Much of this week's rally had been attributed to rumours that crude loading progammes in June would be decimated, tightening supply and supporting prices.

However, the details showed a drop of only four cargoes from May in the Brent-Ninian system fields. Traders expected a similarily muted market reaction to the Forties field programme, due to be announced by Friday.
Bearish news on the demand side was met with a similar shrug of the shoulders by the market. Prices held steady despite a crude throughput cut of 20 percent at Texaco's Nerefco refinery in Rotterdam.
The cutback was blamed on poor refinery margins, which have been severely hit by crude's rise, which has not been followed by a parallel increase in the value of refined products.
